# Leviticus 7 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

This chapter completes the "law of the offerings" section (Lev 6:8–7:38). It gives supplementary priestly regulations for the guilt offering (vv. 1–10), peace offering (vv. 11–21, 28–36), prohibitions on fat and blood (vv. 22–27), and closes with a summary of all five major offerings (vv. 37–38).

---

## Verses 1–2 — The Guilt Offering: Slaughter and Blood

**v. 1: "Now this is the law of the guilt offering, which is most holy"**

- The guilt (trespass/reparation) offering was described for the laity in Lev 5:14–6:7. Here supplemental priestly instructions are given (Precept Austin, citing Rooker). https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_7_commentary
- "Most holy" (Hebrew *qodesh qodashim*) means wholly devoted to sacred use — either to the Lord or to His priests. Bush comments the phrase conveys that these offerings "were to be ranked in their estimation among the 'most holy things'" (Precept Austin). https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_7_commentary
- Gill: The guilt offering was "most holy" — wholly devoted for sacred use, either to the Lord or to His priests. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm
- Guzik: "A trespass is the unlawful crossing of a boundary. God has certain boundaries for humanity…and when they cross those boundaries it is a sin of trespass." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Haydock (Catholic): Trespasses for which these offerings were made "were less offences, than those for which the sin-offerings were appointed." Sins of commission (*peccata*) and of omission (*delicta*) are equally offensive to God, citing St. Augustine. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-7.html

**v. 2: "The guilt offering must be slaughtered in the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered, and the priest shall sprinkle its blood on all sides of the altar."**

- The slaughter occurred at the north side of the altar of burnt offering (cf. Lev 1:11) (Gill). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm
- The blood was sprinkled (or "dashed," per Peake's) around the altar — unlike the sin offering, the blood of the guilt offering did not need to be brought into the tabernacle (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Rooker notes the sprinkling of blood against the altar is one of the few things distinguishing the guilt offering from the sin offering (Precept Austin). https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_7_commentary
- Jewish tradition: a scarlet thread was drawn around the middle of the altar; blood of some sacrifices was sprinkled below it, others above it — the guilt offering's blood was sprinkled above (Gill). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm

---

## Verses 3–5 — The Fat Portions of the Guilt Offering

**v. 3: "And all the fat from it shall be offered: the fat tail, the fat that covers the entrails"**

- Guzik: When the guilt offering is described in chapter 5, nothing is said about what to do with the blood or fat. Here those details are supplied. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Adam Clarke clarified "all its fat" as "chiefly the fat that was found in a detached state, not mixed with the muscles" (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Gill: The "rump" or fat tail of sheep and rams in those countries was very large and fat. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm

**v. 4: "both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver, which is to be removed with the kidneys"**

- The fatty parts listed are the same as those specified for the peace offering in Lev 3. These represent the richest, best portions — all belonging to God.
- Gill notes the fat "upon the flanks" is distinct from the fat on the kidneys; these were "great collops of it" (citing Job 15:27). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm

**v. 5: "The priest shall burn them on the altar as an offering made by fire to the LORD; it is a guilt offering."**

- The burning of the fat was properly "the offering to the Lord" — all the rest belonged to the priest (Gill). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm
- Precept Austin: The guilt offering is the only offering stipulating restitution — either to the sanctuary or to any offended person. It "satisfies not only divine disapproval…but also restores a measure of justice and equity in the material world" (citing Hess). https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_7_commentary

---

## Verses 6–7 — Who May Eat; Similarity to Sin Offering

**v. 6: "Every male among the priests may eat of it. It must be eaten in a holy place; it is most holy."**

- Only male priests — not their wives or daughters — could eat (Gill). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm
- It had to be eaten within the court of the tabernacle, not taken home (Gill). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm
- Guzik: The blood and fat belonged to God; the meat portions could be shared among the priests. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Gill draws a New Testament parallel: "only sanctified persons, true believers, who are made priests unto God, have a right to eat of the altar Christ" (cf. Heb 13:10). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm

**v. 7: "The guilt offering is like the sin offering; the same law applies to both. It belongs to the priest who makes atonement with it."**

- Ellicott: What is omitted in the regulation of one must be supplied from the directions given for the other. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/7.htm
- Rooker (via Precept Austin): The sprinkling of blood against the altar and the description as an offering by fire are all that distinguish the guilt offering from the sin offering. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_7_commentary
- Gill: The officiating priest who made atonement was to receive it — though other priests on duty ate with him. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm

---

## Verses 8–10 — Priestly Portions from Burnt and Grain Offerings

**v. 8: "As for the priest who presents a burnt offering for anyone, the hide of that offering belongs to him."**

- In the burnt offering, the entire animal was consumed on the altar. Only the skin remained, and it became the officiating priest's (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Ellicott: During the Second Temple period, all skins of "most holy things" went to officiating priests, while skins of "holy things" (peace offerings) belonged to the owners. These skins accumulated during the week and were divided among the priests on Sabbath evening. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/7.htm
- Haydock (Catholic): "Of these skins a great profit was made" (citing Philo). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-7.html
- Gill notes the Hebrew emphasizes "to himself" — other priests did not share in this particular perquisite. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm

**v. 9: "Likewise, every grain offering that is baked in an oven or cooked in a pan or on a griddle belongs to the priest who presents it"**

- These three preparation methods were first mentioned in Lev 2:4–7. Here it is clarified that a portion belongs to the officiating priest (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Guzik notes that the early church father Origen allegorized these three cooking methods as the threefold sense of Scripture (literal, moral, mystical) — but John Trapp cautioned against "this itch of allegorising." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/

**v. 10: "and every grain offering, whether dry or mixed with oil, belongs equally to all the sons of Aaron."**

- "Dry" means without oil (as with the poor man's sin offering, Lev 5:11). Whether with or without oil, it was to be equally divided among all priests (Gill). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm
- Guzik: The officiating priest was responsible for distribution, but had to ensure equal portions. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/

---

## Verses 11–14 — The Peace Offering: Bread and Cakes

**v. 11: "Now this is the law of the peace offering that one may present to the LORD"**

- The peace offering was first described in Lev 3 (the mechanics). Here Lev 7:11–21 supplements that with priestly directions. Three subtypes are specified: thanksgiving, vow, and freewill (Ellicott). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/7.htm
- Precept Austin: The peace offering was the only one lay people were allowed to eat. It was "a special time of joyful communion between the offering priest, God, and the offerer" (citing Baker). https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_7_commentary

**v. 12: "If he offers it in thanksgiving, then along with the sacrifice of thanksgiving he shall offer unleavened cakes mixed with olive oil, unleavened wafers coated with oil, and well-kneaded cakes of fine flour mixed with oil."**

- The thanksgiving offering was made to express thanks for unexpected blessing or deliverance (Precept Austin). https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_7_commentary
- Gill (citing Jewish tradition): There were ten of each kind of cake — thirty in total — with specified amounts of flour and oil. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm

**v. 13: "Along with his peace offering of thanksgiving he is to present an offering with cakes of leavened bread."**

- This is the only sacrifice where leavened bread was permitted — but it was not burned on the altar (Lev 2:11 prohibited leaven on the altar). It was eaten as part of the fellowship meal (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Guzik sees rich symbolism: the peace offering had unleavened bread (God's perfection) in one hand and leavened bread (human imperfection) in the other — picturing reconciliation between God and His people. He connects this to Ephesians 2:14 — Christ Himself is our peace, breaking down the wall between Jew and Gentile. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- G. Campbell Morgan (via Guzik): "The Godward side can only be symbolised by that which is unleavened…On the other hand, there remains in man much of imperfection. This is symbolised by the leavened cakes." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/

**v. 14: "From the cakes he must present one portion of each offering as a contribution to the LORD. It belongs to the priest who sprinkles the blood of the peace offering."**

- The "contribution" (or "heave offering," Hebrew *terumah*) was one cake from each kind lifted up before the Lord. Guzik: "So called, because it was heaved and lifted up before the Lord, in token that they received all from him" (citing Trapp). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Adam Clarke (via Guzik): The heave offering was "moved up and down," while the wave offering was moved "from right to left." Both signified acknowledgment of God's provision. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Haydock (Catholic): One loaf representing all the rest was offered as first-fruits — a heave offering, not a sacrifice. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-7.html

---

## Verses 15–18 — When the Meat Must Be Eaten

**v. 15: "The meat of the sacrifice of his peace offering of thanksgiving must be eaten on the day he offers it; none of it may be left until morning."**

- The thanksgiving offering had the strictest time limit — same day only. Guzik: "Thanks must be returned while mercies are fresh; lest, as fish, they putrify with keeping" (citing Trapp). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Whedon (Methodist): The right shoulder and wave breast were eaten by priests and their families; the remainder was returned to the offerer to eat with family and friends — "denoting that they were admitted to a state of intimate companionship with God." This "strikingly prefigures the Lord's Supper, rightly called the Holy Eucharist, or Thanksgiving." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/leviticus-7.html

**v. 16: "If, however, the sacrifice he offers is a vow or a freewill offering, it shall be eaten on the day he presents his sacrifice, but the remainder may be eaten on the next day."**

- A vow offering fulfilled a promise made to God; a freewill offering was entirely spontaneous (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- These were given an extra day for consumption — a concession perhaps because they were products of the offerer's own spontaneity (Keil & Delitzsch, as noted in search excerpt).
- Gill notes the meat was to *begin* being eaten the same day, but need not be finished; leftovers could be eaten the next day. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm

**v. 17: "But any meat of the sacrifice remaining until the third day must be burned up."**

- Burning prevented putrefaction or superstitious uses (Gill). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: The burning on the third day was commanded "to guard against the danger of a desecration of the meal," not simply to compel generosity to the poor (as Theodoret and others suggested). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-7.html
- Guzik: God's desire was for a "fresh," current relationship — not stale leftovers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/

**v. 18: "If any of the meat from his peace offering is eaten on the third day, it will not be accepted. It will not be credited to the one who presented it; it shall be an abomination, and the one who eats of it shall bear his iniquity."**

- The Hebrew word translated "abomination" is *piggul*, meaning a stench — applied only to sacrificial flesh that had become putrid (Keil & Delitzsch excerpt). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-7.html
- Ellicott: "The owner of the sacrifice was responsible for the due observance of this injunction. If, through his neglect, any one ate of the sacrifice after the limited time…the efficacy of the sacrifice was disannulled, and the offerer had to bring another votive offering." https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/7.htm
- Gill: "It shall not be accounted a righteous action, or the offerer receive any benefit by it." https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm
- Gill also notes a typological nuance: perhaps the third-day burning "may have some respect…to the resurrection of Christ on the third day, having seen no corruption." https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm

---

## Verses 19–21 — Ceremonial Purity Required

**v. 19: "Meat that touches anything unclean must not be eaten; it is to be burned up. As for any other meat, anyone who is ceremonially clean may eat it."**

- Gill clarifies that "all that be clean" means not only the owners but anyone the offerer invited — as long as they were ceremonially clean. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm
- Haydock (Catholic): People might eat ordinary flesh touched by something unclean (Deut 12:15, 22), but sacrificial victims defiled by accident had to be burned. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-7.html

**v. 20: "But if anyone who is unclean eats meat from the peace offering that belongs to the LORD, that person must be cut off from his people."**

- "Cut off" (*karet*) could mean excommunication from the covenant community, premature death by divine judgment, or both (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Guzik applies this to New Testament believers: "We cannot enjoy the peace of God until we have received His cleansing grace." He connects it to 1 Corinthians 11:27–32 — partaking of the Lord's Supper unworthily. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Rooker (via Guzik): "Like the Israelite who ate the sacrifice in a state of uncleanness, the believer who partakes of the Lord's Supper in an unworthy state may expect the direct judgment of God." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/

**v. 21: "If one touches anything unclean, whether human uncleanness, an unclean animal, or any unclean, detestable thing, and then eats any of the meat of the peace offering that belongs to the LORD, that person must be cut off from his people."**

- "Human uncleanness" covers issues, dead bodies, etc. (Lev 15; Num 19) (Gill). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm
- The Targum of Jonathan (via Gill) interprets "abominable unclean thing" as unclean reptiles (cf. Lev 11:20). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm
- Guzik: The strong penalty of excommunication was reserved for those who *knowingly* ate while unclean. If done accidentally, a sacrifice was available (Lev 5:2). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/

---

## Verses 22–27 — Prohibition of Fat and Blood

**v. 22–23: "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'Speak to the Israelites and say, "You are not to eat any of the fat of an ox, a sheep, or a goat."'"**

- This repeats and expands the law of Lev 3:17 (Gill). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm
- Guzik: The prohibition was not arbitrary. Fat represented the animal's "goodness and abundance" — the stored energy of the animal. Both belonged to God alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- The law applied to animals used for common food, not just sacrificial animals (Gill). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm
- Maimonides (via Gill) observed that the punishment of "cutting off" was attached because people considered fat a delicacy. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm

**v. 24: "The fat of an animal found dead or mauled by wild beasts may be used for any other purpose, but you must not eat it."**

- Such carcasses were already forbidden for eating (Lev 22:8); the fat was doubly prohibited (Gill). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm
- The fat could be used for practical purposes — medicine, plasters, candles, greasing — but not consumed (Gill). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm

**v. 25: "If anyone eats the fat of an animal from which an offering made by fire may be presented to the LORD, the one who eats it must be cut off from his people."**

- This applies specifically to the fat of sacrificial species (ox, sheep, goat). Rooker (via Guzik) notes that nineteen offenses in the OT resulted in "being cut off," including violation of holy days, moral offenses, eating blood, and failure to circumcise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/

**v. 26: "You must not eat the blood of any bird or animal in any of your dwellings."**

- "In any of your dwellings" means this prohibition applied everywhere, not only at the sanctuary (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- The Rabbis (via Haydock) excepted the blood of fishes since it is not specified. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-7.html

**v. 27: "If anyone eats blood, that person must be cut off from his people."**

- Guzik: Blood represents the life of the animal (Lev 17:11–14), and life belongs to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Trapp (via Guzik): "One would think this to be but a peccadillo [little sin]: yet how fearfully is it threatened! No sin can be little, because there is no little God to sin against." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/

---

## Verses 28–34 — The Priests' Portions: Wave Breast and Heave Thigh

**v. 29–30: "Anyone who presents a peace offering … with his own hands he is to bring the offerings made by fire … he shall bring the fat, together with the breast, and wave the breast as a wave offering before the LORD."**

- "His own hands" — the Israelite could not delegate this. He personally brought the offering (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Keil & Delitzsch: The breast-piece (*chazeh*, brisket) "consists for the most part of cartilaginous fat…and is one of the most savoury parts." It was presented to the Lord as a wave offering (*tenuphah*) and then transferred to the priests. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-7.html
- The waving ceremony: the priest placed his hands under the offerer's hands and moved them horizontally — forward toward the altar (symbolizing presentation to God) and backward (symbolizing reception back as a gift to the priests) (Keil & Delitzsch). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-7.html
- Whedon (Methodist): This was "a presentation to God, who rules in heaven above and in the earth beneath." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/leviticus-7.html

**v. 31: "The priest is to burn the fat on the altar, but the breast belongs to Aaron and his sons."**

- The breast (wave offering) went to the priesthood as a whole — all the sons of Aaron.

**v. 32–33: "And you are to give the right thigh to the priest as a contribution from your peace offering. The son of Aaron who presents the blood and fat of the peace offering shall have the right thigh as a portion."**

- Unlike the breast (for all priests), the right thigh went specifically to the officiating priest (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Keil & Delitzsch: "Thigh" (*shoq*) is the hind-leg, or the upper part (ham) — a particularly savory portion, as seen in 1 Samuel 9:24. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-7.html
- The thigh was a "heave offering" (*terumah*), lifted vertically, whereas the breast was "waved" (*tenuphah*), moved horizontally (Keil & Delitzsch). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-7.html

**v. 34: "I have taken from the sons of Israel the breast of the wave offering and the thigh of the contribution of their peace offerings, and I have given them to Aaron the priest and his sons as a permanent portion from the sons of Israel."**

- Guzik: "Both portions belonged to the LORD. God was not visibly present at the sacrifice, yet God still received the offering through the work of the appointed, anointed priest. God received the offering, then gave it to the priest." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Haydock (Catholic): The breast was "separated…for the Lord, and waved before Him." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-7.html

---

## Verses 35–36 — The Priests' Permanent Portion

**v. 35: "This is the portion of the offerings made by fire to the LORD for Aaron and his sons since the day they were presented to serve the LORD as priests."**

- Keil & Delitzsch: The Hebrew word translated "portion" (*mishchah*) here does not mean "anointing" but "share" — a measuring off, from the Aramaic/Arabic root meaning to measure. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-7.html

**v. 36: "On the day they were anointed, the LORD commanded that this be given them by the sons of Israel. It is a permanent portion for the generations to come."**

- Guzik: Though these sacrifices were given to the Lord, portions belonged to the priests "by right and by command." The priests (tribe of Levi) had no land inheritance (Num 18:20); God was their inheritance, and they were provided for by the offerings of God's people. This principle carries into the New Testament: "those who serve God and His people in spiritual ways have the right to be supported in material ways" (1 Cor 9:12–14). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/

---

## Verses 37–38 — Summary Postscript

**v. 37: "This is the law of the burnt offering, the grain offering, the sin offering, the guilt offering, the ordination offering, and the peace offering"**

- This verse lists six offerings, adding the "ordination offering" (consecration offering) to the five main sacrifices. This ordination offering is described in Leviticus 8 (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/
- Haydock (Catholic): "Six sorts of sacrifices are here specified: holocausts, flour-offerings, sin and trespass-offerings, those for the consecration of priests, and the peace-offerings." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-7.html

**v. 38: "which the LORD gave Moses on Mount Sinai on the day He commanded the Israelites to present their offerings to the LORD in the Wilderness of Sinai."**

- This concluding verse anchors all the sacrificial legislation to the Sinai revelation, underscoring its divine authority.
- Guzik notes this is a summary statement for the previous seven chapters. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/

---

## Notes on Differing Protestant Traditions

**General Observation:** On Leviticus 7, the major Protestant traditions are broadly united in reading the sacrificial system typologically as pointing to Christ. The differences are more in emphasis than in interpretive conclusions.

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word – Guzik):** Emphasizes the experiential dimension: fresh relationship with God, the danger of "stale" fellowship, the need for cleansing before communion, and the Holy Spirit's symbolism in the oil. Strong application to the Lord's Supper. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-7/

- **Reformed/Evangelical (Precept Austin):** Emphasizes the guilt offering as Christ's atonement. Quotes William MacDonald: "As our trespass offering, the Lord Jesus not only restored what had been stolen through man's sin, but He added more. For God has received more glory through the finished work of Christ than if sin had never entered the world." https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_7_commentary

- **Methodist/Wesleyan (Whedon):** Emphasizes the eucharistic, thanksgiving dimension. The peace offering is "strikingly prefiguring the Lord's Supper, rightly called the Holy Eucharist, or Thanksgiving, and the blessedness of eating and drinking in the kingdom of God" (citing Luke 14:15). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/leviticus-7.html

- **Baptist (Gill):** Reads the text with attention to Hebrew detail and rabbinic sources. Emphasizes the portions as divinely appointed dues. Draws careful typological connections (e.g., the third day pointing to Christ's resurrection). https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/7.htm

- **Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch):** Emphasizes the sacrificial meal as "a holy covenant meal, a meal of love and joy, which represented domestic fellowship with the Lord," shadowing forth "the blessedness of eating and drinking in the kingdom of God" (Luke 13:15; 22:30). Detailed attention to the ritual mechanics of waving and heaving. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-7.html

- **Anglican (Ellicott):** Careful text-critical and historical notes (e.g., Second Temple practices regarding skins). Attention to the offerer's responsibilities and the consequences of neglect. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/7.htm

---

## Catholic Reading (Haydock)

- Distinguishes trespasses as "less offences" than those requiring sin offerings, yet equally offensive to God (citing St. Augustine). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-7.html
- Notes that the leavened bread was for priestly use, not altar sacrifice. The heave offering represented first-fruits, "not as a sacrifice." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-7.html
- Observes that "by neglecting to comply exactly with God's commands, we lose the fruits of our former piety" (v. 18). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-7.html
- On v. 30, notes that the priest directed the offerer's hands "to form a triple cross" (citing Cajetan and Tirinus) — a traditional Catholic typological reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-7.html

---

## Modern Scholarship (Peake's Commentary)

- Peake's notes that the blood is "dashed (not sprinkled) round the altar." The fat is carefully removed and offered to Yahweh. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-7.html
- Observes the priests' dues are the same for guilt and sin offerings: "Every guilt offering is also a sin offering, though the reverse…is not the case." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-7.html
- Notes comparative evidence: in the sacrificial tariffs of Marseilles and Sippar the hide goes to priests; at Carthage, to the offerer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-7.html
- Suggests the limitation of the festival to two days may be "a reminiscence of the early limitation of the duration of a festival to two days." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-7.html
- On vv. 19–21: "The caution was doubtless necessitated by the licence of the older sacrifices, where the circumstances of the feasts might easily be…conducive to much worse things than ritual uncleanness. Hence the sternness of the tone here." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-7.html
